welfare and progress of this country, and if the hon. gentleman sees fit to administer that department, as he has lightly suggested-I think rather in humorous terms than with wrong intent-if that is his intention, then I say he has made a more violent accusation against the good faith and sound patriotism of the Government of which he is a member than any member of this House ever .made before.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow some of the statements which have been made by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) to go unchallenged. My hon. friend has undertaken to refer, in answer to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche), to certain arrests that were made in the province of Saskatchewan in the by-election two years ago. I want to tell the hon. member for Edmonton that while a very large number of arrests were made, no charge was preferred against any man who was arrested according to the law in this or any British country in the known world. Take the case of this man Smythe who was arrested; he was not faced by a magistrate upon the charge with which he was arrested at all. Numbers of other homestead inspectors were arrested, and when they were arrested, without the issue of a warrant, they were arrested largely on the strength of a telegram from a whisky detective in the city of Regina.
Will the hon. gentleman give the names of those other men who were arrested?
I will be glad to supply my hon. friend with them. I do not have them here. I will name one who was arrested-Mr. Shields.
Was he a homestead inspector?

He was a homestead inspector. He was arrested at some distance up the line from Regina, handcuffed, paraded in the train from there to Regina, and cast into jail at that place. Bail was asked and urged, but it was denied. The matter was taken before one of the justices of the High Court, wno commented upon the conduct of those in charge of the case and expressed the hope that the people of Saskatchewan were not prepared to conform to Russian methods. Therefore, he would undertake to liberate Mr. Shields, and he said that if the men in charge of the jail did not obey his orders

he and Mr. Johnston would go down to the jail themselves and see that Mr. Shields was liberated from the cell in which he had been placed by the officers of the Liberal Government of the province. Mr. Shields was allowed to go, but a moment afterwards he was re-arrested and put in jail again. The same justice ordered his release at once and Mr. Shields went home. He came back for trial at the time appointed and no charge was preferred against him; he was told to go, as they had nothing to offer against him and no charge to prefer. This condition of affairs obtained in other cases in connection with arrests that were made in that election. There were very many-
How many?

The only case in which a' fine was imposed by a justice of the peace was that against a homestead inspector by the name of Smythe, and that conviction was obtained on an entirely different charge from the one on which he had been arrested.
What was he fined for?

He was fined on some
trivial charge; I do not recall it. I have not read the case for over a year and I do not recall to memory what the charge was, but I will promise my hon. friends on the other side of this House that before the vote upon this debate is taken I will submit a history of the arrests in that particular province and I am sure it will startle the good sense not only of hon. gentlemen opposite, but the people of this Dominion. My hon. friend the member for Edmonton rose with righteous indignation in respect to the administration of the Department of the Interior and the action of officers of that department in taking part in elections in the western provinces of Canada. I am free to confess that there is and always has been a condition of affairs that apparently has admitted of officials taking a certain part in elections in those provinces. There is probably no man in this Dominion of Canada more responsible for that condition of affairs than is my hon. friend the member for Edmonton himself.
It will be, I am sure, in the recollection of certain hon. members of this House, especially of my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), that in the year 1896 a resolution was introduced and an understanding arrived at between both sides of this House, which carried with it a perfect understanding that
officials of the Government were not to take part in elections. I think this is what was laid down by my right hon. friend-I take it from ' Hansard ' of 1896, Volume 1:
That, whilst it is desirable that every official in the employ of the Government of Canada should enjoy perfect freedom of political opinions and the untrammelled exercise of his franchise in accord therewith, no official should be engaged or be permitted to engage in partisan work of any description in the election of a representative to a provinical or Dominion legislature.
This, I understand, was approved and accepted by both sides of the House. I have not in mind whether it was carefully observed and carried out, but I know that, when an election was called for provincial purposes in the province of Saskatchewan at the time of the foundation of that province in 1905, my hon. friend the member for Edmonton, who stands up to-day in righteous indignation condemns the taking part in the political warfare of any province of the officers of any particular department, if the press quotes him correctly, is reported, not only as being in the province of Saskatchewan assisting in that contest, but as undertaking to give out a published interview as appearing in the press of that province of that day. What did he say then? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to compare his words at that time in the province of Saskatchewan, when he was engaged in the first election of 1905, with the speech with which he has just favoured the House this afternoon. As I understand it, he is speaking of the officers of the Department of the Interior and dealing with this same resolution that was approved by both sides of the House. His interview in part is as follows; he is referring to homestead inspectors and others:
They have the power of speech and therefore they are entitled to express their political opinions. They are entitled to express them to homesteaders; they are entitled to express them to men under their control; they are entitled to go on the public platform and express them as presidents and officers of Liberal organizations.
Might I ask my hon. friend the authority for that interview?
My hon. friend will find it in the public press of Saskatchewan of that day.
What paper was it published in??
I will try to get my hon. friend a copy, I simply copied this out of the paper some time ago.

Before my hon. friend
goes any further, I wish to say that such a statement as being made by me is absolutely false.

I shall be glad to provide my hon. friend with a press report of it, and he will satisfy himself in the matter. My hon. friend talks about the responsibility resting upon an officer of the department and especially upon a minister who is responsible for the administration of a department. If my hon. friend is not satisfied with the statement in respect to the interview which I have quoted, probably he will be satisfied with an official record of the department, by which record he, as Minister of the Interior, divested himself of all rights and of all powers in respect to the form of appointments made for the filling of positions in the western provinces of Canada. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior has mentioned here to-day the name of one R. E. A. Leech, a gentleman whose name is fast becoming a household word in various parts of this Dominion, largely by reason of the services which he has been able to render the hon. gentlemen opposite, and by reason of the generous compensation which he has received in various forms from the public treasury for services so rendered. That gentleman was the Liberal organizer of the province of Manitoba when that famous scheme of the thin red line was practised by which thousands of the best citizens of that province were deprived of their right and of their liberty to exercise the franchise. How was that effort of Mr. Leech appreciated by the Government of hon. gentlemen opposite in those days? I am quoting from a public record how he was appreciated by no less a person than my hon. friend the member for Edmonton who issued this instruction, dated Ottawa, March 23, 1906:
Memorandum.
Mr. K. E. A. Leech,-With a view to securing more efficient service in office and field work in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, you are hereby given authority to . suspend, for cause and for such time as deemed . advisable, any Dominion Lands agent, clerk, homestead inspector, sub-agent, or other employee in the service of the Lands Branch of the Department of the Interior. You will .promptly report to head office each case of such *Suspension, giving full particulars as to the reasons for the action taken, when the matter will be dealt with by the department.
(Sgd.) Frank Oliver.
In view of these conditions, in view of file appointment of men under such a head and Under such an officer of the department as Mr. R. E. A. Leech, is it any

wonder that a practice should have been established in those western provinces whereby the officials of the Department of the Interior in particular have from time to time taken part in political contests? I am frank in admitting that it is becoming a very common practice. As my friend the Minister of the Interior said, before the present Government took office, you could not go into any constituency without being met by a horde of Liberal employees taking part in, taking charge of and managing the political campaign of the Liberal party.
In so far as the accusation of my hon. friend from Humbolt (Mr. Neely) is concerned, I was not in the House when he was speaking and I did not hear of it. All that I have to say in respect to Mr. Campbell is that he was for some time a member of this House. I understand that he is an efficient official. If he is guilty of this particular charge, which my hon. friend has made against him, it is a matter of great surprise and of great regret to me. I can only hope and only promise hon. gentlemen opposite that in elections in western Canada, as far as officers of any department of the Government are concerned, they will receive a great deal better treatment, and I hope perfect treatment, as compared with the treatment which we received when we had to go into these contests.
On the motion of Mr. Foster for Committee of Supply:

I wish, Mr. Speaker, to invite the attention of the House to a matter of very great importance, especially to. the people of eastern Canada; and I propose, before resuming my seat to conclude with the motion of which I have given my hon. friend the Minister of Customs notice. A year ago or so I took occasion, availing myself of the privilege accorded to me as a member of this House, to call the attention of hon. members and of the country to the trend of events with respect to legislation in Canada. On that occasion, I illustrated my viewpoint by calling to the attention of the House several Bills which were simply Bills of an enabling character, Bills giving power to the Governor in Council to legislate in respect to the matter they referred to. I think I pointed out that the Naval Bill was an enabling statute, that the Highways Bill, the Bill relating to Branch Lines, the Agricultural Bill, were all

enabling statutes, that all gave power to the Governor in Council to legislate with regard to matters that should be under the direct control of the people of the country through their representatives. I called attention to the fact that in one particular Bill, namely, that relating to railway construction and railway acquisition, it was an enabling statute giving the Minister of Railways-not merely the Governor in Council, but the Minister of Railways power and authority to do in this respect that which should be performed and controlled by the Parliament of Canada. I think that in some measure I illustrated the dangers incident to legislation by Order in Council. I pointed out that it meant that we were going back in history and doing over again under this Administration what had been done when we were mere colonies under the Crown and under the direction of a Governor in Council who legislated in a large measure for the people. I thought at that time, and I still think, that that class of legislation is against the best interests of Canada. But we have developed very recently a method of legislation in Canada that is much more dangerous and much more inimical to the public interest than that of the Order in Council. I refer to orders made by the Board of Customs of Canada. That is a much more dangerous form of legislation, because of the secrecy of its character, and the subtlety of its nature, and because it is surreptitious in the method pursued, it legislates in respect to matters which should be under the control of Parliament and should be subject to public discussion and within the knowledge of the whole people. An illustration of this is to be found in a case which has developed within the last few days. To an inquiry I made I received an answer from the Minister of Customs to the effect that no Order in Council had been passed whereby the importation of slag into Canada was affected, but that there had been an order of the Customs Board, passed in September last which imposed, or had the effect of imposing, a duty on what is known as basic slag. I need not recite the question and answer. The minister made a statement with respect to the order of the Customs Board, and he placed in my hands for the information of hon. members the following:
Meeting of the Board of Customs held, Ottawa, 9th September, 1913.
Question of duty on basic furnace slag, ground.
Declared to be dutiable under tariff item 663 and in effect from 9th November, 1913.
John McDougald,
Chairman.

Is basic slag the raw
material, that is, the product of the steel mill?

It is a raw material, ground material, but that will develop as I proceed. Accompanying this order of the Customs Board was the following memorandum-or at least that was furnished me after I had first received a copy of the order. The order on its face seems to have dropped into the groove in which the Customs Board would meet: there is nothing preliminary to show any initiative with respect to this order. There was no application; apparently it dropped from the heavens, without being put in motion by anybody.

Is the hon. gentleman
finding fault with anything that dropped from the heavens?

I should be very
happy to congratulate the hon. gentleman if I thought he came from that direction.
That is where he is going.
To the Senate.

I am sure we hope he
will get there; I am afraid that if he keeps the company he is now keeping, there may some doubt with regard to his ultimate destination. This memorandum, which is dated February 6, 1914, reads as follows:
The question of the duty on basic slag, ground, was referred to the Board of Customs, 9th September, 1913, under section 5S of the Customs Act, on the verbal representations of the manager of the Cross Fertilizers Company, who claims that the company has a capital of $140,000 invested in the manufacture of ground basic slag at Sydney, N.S., and that in 1912 they manufactured 16,000 tons of this article. Respectfully submitted,
John McDougald, Commissioner of Customs.
I do not propose to analyse that memorandum, or to comment upon it. It says that the Board of Customs took action under t'he 58th section of the Customs Act of Canada with respect to a commodity referred to in the order as basic furnace slag, ground. For many years, down to November 9 last, under the provisions of the customs tariff of 1907, blast furnace slag came into Canada free of all customs impost.
Mr. A. IC. MACLEAN: What is the number of the tariff item?

372. Under the order passed on September 9 this was made dutiable under item 663 of the tariff, which reads as follows:
Fertilizers, compounded or manufactured, n.o.p., 5 per cent British preferential tariff, 7i per cent intermediate tariff, 10 per cent general tariff.
I wish to read, and to ask hon. members of this House to note the reading of it, the 58t'h section of the Customs Tariff Act, under which this order was passed:
Whenever any difference arises or when even any doubt exists as to any or what rate of duty is payable on any class of goods, and there is no previous decision upon the question by any competent tribunal, binding throughout Canada, the Board of Customs may declare the rate of duty payable on the class of goods in question, or that such goods are exempt from duty, subject in each case to an appeal, by any person interested, to the Governor in Council, and any such declaration of the Board of Customs when approved by the minister, or any such declaration when made by any Order in Council upon appeal, shall have force and effect as if the same had been sanctioned by statute.
This is a provision of the statute which enables the Customs Board, under certain conditions, to vary and control certain items of the tariff. I hold that the order passed in September last is not in accord with the statute. Under the provisions of the statute, any declaration so made by the Board of Customs shall have force and effect only when approved by the Minister, and it must therefore appear on the face of the order that there were doubts or differences in respect of the subject matter of the order, which, when passed, requires the approval of the minister and can only be made effective by that approval being made part of the order. Therefore in my judgment the order itself is illegal and improper.
I want to say that this is a dangerous method of making conditions with respect to the importation of anything into this country. I admit that the order refers to basic furnace slag, ground, whilst item 372 of the tariff mentions blast furnace slag.
Does the order refer to the number of this item?

No, it makes no reference to item 372; it simply says: 'duty on basic furnace slag, ground,' Under the provisions of item 372, blast furnace slag has been imported into Canada for many years free of duty. It will be observed that item 372 does not say that blast furnace slag is free only when unground; it does not refer to it in anyway as being ground or unground. I can only infer that a dis-

tinction is made between blast furnace slag and basic furnace slag, ground. I hold, in the first place, that the Board of Customs had no jurisdiction to deal with the matter, that they have not followed the statute, that the provisions and conditions of that statute have not been observed by them or recognized by them. We all know and it is well understood that wherever a tribunal is created by statute the terms of the statute must be strictly followed in order to give jurisdiction to that tribunal. A statutory court has jurisdiction and authority only when the provisions of the statute are rigidly followed and strictly adhered to. It must be shown on the face of the proceedings that that has been done. In this instance there is no such showing, it does not appear that they had jurisdiction, and my contention is that under that order any duty that has been collected by the Customs of Canada to-day on blast furnace slag imported into Canada is collected unjustifiably and without authority of law, and not in any way ratified by the action of the board itself.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Bill No. 51, respecting the Bronson Company.-Mr. Fripp.
Bill No. 52, respecting the Central Railway Company of Canada.-Mr. W. H. Bennett.
Bill No. 53, respecting the Empire Life Insurance Company of Canada.-Mr. Mae-donell.
Bill No. 54, respecting the Niagara-Welland Power Company.-Mr. Blain.
Bill No. 55, respecting the Quinze and Blanche Railway Company.-Mr. Fripp.

Before
recess, I was referring to the object of this order of the Customs Board, and in doing so I had remarked on the very great injustice and the secrecy of it. For many years slag has been used by the farmers in conjunction with other commodities as a fertilizer. The slag is brought in, in a ground form and is then combined with nitrates and potash. I presume the phosphorous in the slag has certain fertilizing qualities. The farmer mixes these commodities together on his barn floor and utilizes the compound as

a fertilizer. The effect of the order of the board has been very material, and has caused very serious surprise. It was not made the subject matter of a tariff discussion in this House, nor was it even subject matter of an application made on behalf of some association. Nothing was heard of it, until, suddenly, out of a clear sky came the intelligence that there had been imposed upon this article a customs tariff of 10 per cent in the case of general importation, and in the case of preferential, a duty of 5 per cent. Slag is a by-product of steel manufacture. It is a sort of cinder and can be used in the form in which it comes from the factory, as a fertilizer for grass lands, but not so effectively as if it were crushed by the farmer. When ground, it is more effective as it reaches more roots of the grass or grain, as the case may be.
Does this basic slag add any fertility to the soil?

It is used for root
crops in a mixture that the chemical fertilizing companies make of slag, nitrates and potash. In its crude form, that is, just as it is taken from the refuse of the mill, it has a fertilizing effect on grass lands, at least, it is so claimed, and it has been used by the farmers, particularly in Eastern Canada, for that purpose. I may say it is also used by the orchardists of Nova Scotia in the Annapolis Valley. I will have occasion a little later on to refer to the transactions of that body with respect to this matter. I believe that a fruit grower from Nova Scotia appeared before the Agricultural Committee of this House last session and gave evidence before the Committee with respect to the importation of slag to the Nova Scotia orchardists.

I do not think the
hon. gentleman understands my question. Does slag add to the fertility of the soil, or is it its chemical action on the soil that gives slag its value?

I am not expert
enough to explain that to my hon. friend. I know it is used as a plant food.

I hardly think it is
a plant food. It is used for its chemical effect.

At any rate, I can
tell my hon. friend that the farmers spread it on their grass lands and I presume they do so because it helps in the growing of their crops. Slag is also used for making
blocks and in connection with road making, and it used to be brought into Canada, under clause 372 of the tariff, free of duty. The order of the Customs Board transferred it from clause 372 to item 663, ' fertilizers compounded or manufactured,' and imposed a duty on it. The question might arise, and I presume it was in the minds of the Customs Board, as to whether this was a manufactured fertilizer.
It is not a fertilizer.

The Customs Board
have treated it as a fertilizer.
I understand it only helps the farmer to mine the soil; it is not a fertilizer at all.

Then on the statement of the hon. gentleman, the action of the Board of Customs in making it subject to duty under item 663, which covers fertilizers compounded or manufactured, was without any excuse whatever. I was going on to discuss the question as to whether the mere grinding or crushing of the slag made it a manufactured article. It is a question about which there may be a difference of opinion. My own judgment would be that it is not a manufactured article when so treated any more than ashes brought in and put upon the land would be if the ashes were sifted. The mere sifting of the ashes or the grinding or the material in no way changes their component parts. The grinding of the slag is for the greater convenience of the farmer in spreading it over his land with the greatest possible effect. My contention in respect to this matter is, first, that whatever was attempted to be done was illegally attempted to be done, and, in the second place, that there is no justification for placing this article under item 663.
But the farmers of eastern Canada, the fruit growers of the Annapolis valley, the farmers of Westmorland county, who have been using this article for years not paying any duty upon it, were astounded on learning that it was subject to duty. They only learned it in November, and I have some evidence to offer with respect to the method by which this was carried out. Here is a duty of 10 per cent placed upon this article. They usually brought it in delivered at Halifax or St. John at $11.50 a ton. Slag brought from Sydney could only be purchased at $11.50 a ton; that is at a price equal to the foreign article delivered at an ocean port. If you would ask quotations for slag from the Sydney people you would be quoted a price of $11.50 at Hali-

fax or at St. John, plus the freight to the point where the article was required. If an Antigonish farmer sought to buy slag at Sydney he would be quoted $11.50. at Halifax, because that is the cost of the foreign article, plus the freight from Halifax to Antigonish. The article was quoted at $11.50 at Halifax in order to meet the foreign competition and in addition to that there would be the freight from Halifax to St. John to the point where the article was required to be used.
That situation confronted the farmer. At the very same moment, and it is strange that they should synchronize, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals' (Mr. Cochrane) imposed an additional freight tariff over the Intercolonial railway of, first, about 40 cents a ton from St. John to Sackville in Westmorland county. The farmer had imposed upon him the burden of this tariff, and in addition to that, by another department of the Government he had exacted from him 40 cents a ton as freight on this very same article. The method pursued is a simple one, whereby with simply turning a screw, an additional amount is extorted from the farming interests of Canada. I am amazed at the ease with which it is accomplished. An effort was made by the farmers of western Canada to get free wheat. They sent large delegations, they sent men who were representative of large agricultural associations, men who came here representing thousands and thousands of farmers asking the Government to give them free wheat. The Government would not listen, but here, according to this, one lone man from Sydney, Cape Breton, accidentally meets the Commissioner of Customs. I am only assuming this. The manager of a fertilizer company down in Sydney makes a quiet request, stealthily, without any public notice being given, that this article which had been brought into Canada free of customs, should be made subject to a duty of 10 per cent, and lo, it is accomplished. This is quietly and secretly turning the screw whereby the Customs revenue of Canada is increased and the burdens of the farmers of Canada are added to. The extent to which this method is adopted, I am informed, is something startling. I have been told on very good authority that the increases by this method during the last two or three years would amount to an addition of one per cent to the average Customs tariff of Canada. Yet the people do not realize it until they are called upon to pay the

duty, because, after all, it is the consumer who has to pay the duty.
This article of which I am speaking is the raw material of the farmer in eastern Canada. He cannot get manure in abundance. The long cold winters make it almost impossible for the farmers to keep very large stocks of cattle. There is a scarcity of fertilizer, and they are compelled to pay to commercial fertilizer companies prices ranging from $25 to $42 per ton. The $42 article is recognized by the intelligent farmer as being more economical than the $25 article because of its richness in fertilizing qualities. They pay in most instances from $40 to $42 a ton for commercial fertilizers. The product of that fertilizing material is not worth, and I am told by intelligent farmers will not realize to them, $42 a ton on wheat or whatever may be the product grown. That is to say, the farmers cannot realize in the first year $42 a ton for the crop which is planted on the area covered by this material. Therefore it is a matter that is of some moment and that is attracting attention.
There is one subject that is being discussed very generally throughout Canada to-day. It is discussed in this House, in the press, on the public platform, by the fireside in the homes of our country, everywhere it is discussed,-I refer to the increased cost of living. Many contributing causes are alleged. I am not going to speak of the causes or to discuss them. Many people in our towns and cities state that one of the causes for the increased cost of living is the lessened production on the farm. The cry goes out from the artisan and the labourer and the mechanic that the farmer is reaping everything; that he is charging too much for the products of his farm and that he is being enriched at the expense of the consumer. They say: Why do you not produce more? They say that the prices of agricultural products such as vegetables, butter and other products that are in general use as necessities of life, are all higher by reason of the fact of under production. The claim is, and I think it is fairly and rightly made, that the farmers, in eastern Canada at least, are not producing to the extent that they should do. That very fact increases the cost of production because the supply is not equal to the demand. The farmers answer that they are doing their utmost, and many of them say that they have not the plant food required to enable them to till their land so that their production can be greater. Another answer has been very fairly made by the

farmers that'because of the restricted markets they are not encouraged and stimulated to further production; that there is a fluctuation and even an uncertainty with respect to a market. That is one of the reasons why I, as an individual, supported reciprocity, because I believe that it would afford an additional market and a choice of markets, thus assuring stability of production, giving assurance to the farmer that if he could not succeed in one market he would succeed in another, and that it would be to his advantage, as it would be to the advantage of a consumer, that the production should be greater and steadier, and therefore the prices would be steadier and more to the satisfaction of the consumer as well as of the producer. It is not to the advantage of the farmer to have a very high price during one year and a very low price during the next year for the same commodity, and it is certainly not of advantage to the consumer. The latter would rather have an assured supply at a steady price than have the supply and the price fluctuate up and down.
That is a mere discussion of the economics involved in this question. The action of the Customs Board, which I hold was not regular because it nowhere appears that the Minister of Customs gave his approval as required under the Act, has indeed resulted to the injury of the farming community in eastern Canada, as I am well informed, and I believe to the farmers generally throughout Canada wherever commercial fertilizers are made and sold.
This slag is used by the commercial fertilizing companies in the manufacture of fertilizing materials in conjunction with other component parts, as I have said, nitrates and potash. These materials are imported from abroad, largely from Chili, Belgium, Germany, the Southern States, etc. The slag and the potash and the nitrates are brought in free under the tariff of Canada. The slag, however, under this order is made subject to a duty. The additional freight rate and the additional duty bear heavily upon the farmers in eastern Canada. To that extent it has an effect upon the production of the farms in eastern Canada, upon the supply of the necessities of life required by the consumers. In that way, it has a natural bearing upon the high cost of living.
I have had the advantage of having this matter placed before me by a very intelligent farmer who comes from my own constituency and whose name, wherever
known, is respected. I can best quote from his letter to me. He says:
One of the several serious handicaps to profitable farming in these two provinces is the low grade quality and excessive prices of most of the fertilizers offered to our farmers. Those well-meaning wise people who do all their farming on paper are continually telling us how easy it would be to double the yield per acre by better methods. But every practical farmer knowsand my informant is a practical farmer; he is not a gentleman farmer in the usual meaning of that term.
-that on our average upland farms, with its more or less exhausted soil, bigger crops cannot be raised, unless more plant-food is supplied to that soil in the shape of fertilizers. The immense cost of feeding cattle through our long winters and occasional short crops of fodder make it impossible for any man to keep sufficient live stock to produce more than a trifling supply of barn manure, totally inadequate for any enlargement of his fields, or increased yields per acre.
How, then, I ask, shall the farmer make good in the face of these facts, and double the fruits of his field? 4 Nothing is easier,' answer the manufacturers. ' See our factories,' they exclaim, * all over these provinces, turning out unlimited quantities and endless variety of fertilizers already mixed, to supply your every want.' 'Buy our mixed fertilizers, Mr. Farmer, double your crops per acre, and get rich quick,' is the slogan of their many agents sent out to push the sale of these goods. Unfortunately for the farmers, however, our tariff maintains a heavy duty on all mixed fertilizers. With this advantage, our Canadian fertilizer companies apparently fix their prices to the farmer on the basis of charging him * all that the traffic will bear,'-$25, $30 and even up to $42 per ton is demanded for these mixed goods. At the same time, our farmers know $1 per ton is the outside market-value of barn manure for common crops. Is it any wonder, then, that the farmers are suspicious of such costly goods and buy so little of them? Is it any wonder farm crops are decreasing in these two provinces when the men who try to grow them are charged $40 to $42 per ton for mixed fertilizer of the standard analysis of 4-8-10, which is the lowest grade any man should use? Forty dollars per, ton! Just think of it! Not one of our principal crops, not even wheat, is worth $40 per ton. At such unreasonable prices, it requires the whole gross proceeds of three to five acres of hay, or of wheat, or of oats, or of barley, to pay the first cost of a single ton of these factory mixed fertilizers, to say nothing of the large cost of raising and harvesting the crop besides. I freely admit there are plenty of mixed fertilizers on market for $30 per ton, or for less. Much of the factory mixed product, however, is of such low grade analysis, and so completely stuffed with 4 fillers ' as to make it even more expensive to those who use them, than the better quality at the bigger price.
I relate now the experience of this gentleman with respect to the treatment of this material:

Having become impressed years ago with our great need of better and cheaper fertilizers, I set out to inform myself if such were nnt obtainable ; and, if so, why these provinces should be deprived of their benefits. Travelling in the Southern States, I found their immense production of cotton, corn, tobacco, sugar cane and garden truck, practically all depended on the lavish use of high-grade fertilizers obtained at a reasonable cost. English farmers have steadily increased their yields per acre by importing guano for the last fifty years from another hemisphere; and now with that supply becoming scarce, they have an abundance of high-grade slag at home at prices nominal, compared with the cost of the same grades here. Being fully convinced that I could double the proceeds from my farm operations if permitted to buy reliable fertilizers at their value in the open market, I determined to make the effort.
One year ago, in conjunction with my brother, A. Chase Faweett, and C. Fred. Fawcett, we set out to buy a few carloads of fertilizers for ourselves and a few neighbours, at what we had learned was something near their real value in the open markets of the world. After weeks of correspondence and many interviews with agents of our Canadian mixed fertilizer companies, we found it impossible to buy their mixed goods at anything near our estimate of their real values. Rather than pay their prices, we decided to buy the several imported ingredients and do our own mixing by hand on our own bam floors. To make a long story short, we soon had six carloads at our station; three of slag direct from England, for our grass and grain, and three of phosphate rock, potash and nitrate, to blend in a 4-8-10 mixture for potatoes and turnips. The best evidence I can give of the complete success of our experiment and the satisfaction we all got by mixing our own fertilizers and knowing just what they contained, is to mention the fact that we are now placing our next spring order for five times as much as last year (or some eight thousand dollars' worth) lor our own and nearby neighbours' use.
There is the result of the experiment of this farmer in eastern Canada. He is voicing the judgment, experience and opinion of all farmers there who have had occasion to purchase commercial fertilizers. With respect to his experiment, he goes on to say:
Much as we saved in purchase money and gained in better crops, however, was only in small comparison with valuable knowledge we acquired in the venture. By carrying on a wide correspondence and by further persistently delving into the mysteries of the fertilizer business, we now find that for next year, we can buy most of these unmixed products for even less money than last year, and possibly save something besides on freight rates and larger orders.
But the increase of duty discounts this very much, as also does the recent increase in Intercolonial freight rates. For he and his associates live along the line of the Intercolonial railway, and the recent increase on this material largely discounts

the advantage they were to- secure by reason of the experiment which they made last year, and the greater knowledge gained by them in study, correspondence and travel. Evidence of that character must of necessity have a very great weight with hon. members of this House, and it must make them realize that the Government of the day, in imposing these additional burdens on the farmers of eastern Canada, have done something which is unjustifiable and against the best interests of the country. If they want to help production, then let the farmer have this material free. This is the farmer's raw material. The protectionist clings to the idea always that, while he should have protection for his manufactured products, the raw material must come in free. That he demands, that he insists upon, and that he secures from any government that is carried on on protectionist lines. The farmer asks that his raw material, this slag, be made free. He goes further- although this may not be pertinent to the discussion of the particular motion I am bringing before the House-he asks that all fertilizers should be made free, because all fertilizers are his raw material out of which he brings forth the manufactured product, the crop. If you want to lessen even in a slight degree the cost of farm products to the labourer, the artisan and the consumer everywhere, make it possible for the farmers to produce their crops at a lower percentage of cost. This can be done always by increased production, and it certainly can be accomplished if you give the farmer his raw material free, and refrain from burdening him with customs duties.
I want to relate some further facts in regard to the manner in which this order was passed by the Board of Customs. (Reading):
We first learned of this proposal to impose such a duty-
That is, the duty that was imposed on the 9th of November.
by accident. We heard it as a rumour first, but now realize that it is all too true. In October we were on the point of closing a contract for 1,000 tons of British or Belgian slag with the Nitrate Agencies Company, New York city. Said slag was to be of extra quality and some dollars per ton cheaper than any ever on our market before. It contained 17 per cent to 19 per cent phosphorus, with 14 per cent guaranteed soluble and available.
Perhaps the hon. member who questioned me. a few moments ago will take that to heart.
Is the hon. gentleman now reading from the same letter as that which he quoted from a few moments ago?

No, from another
letter.
That is not from a farmer?
It is.

And he was buying a
thousand tons for his own use?

For his own use and the use of his neighbours; they were cooperating. This man is a practical farmer, a man of some means, and because of his being a practical farmer, working his farm as it should be worked, he is in a position to give an order for a thousand tons for himself and his associates. I think my hon. friend should not look down upon him or regard him with scorn because he is a practical farmer.
I was not looking down upon him; I simply asked the hon. gentleman a question.

The hon. minister
spoke contemptuously, and in a way in which I would not expect him to speak.
Give him the name.

The name of the gentleman in question is W. B. Fawcett, of Sackville, county of Westmorland. He was born and brought up in a Conservative family. The Fawcett family has been Conservative from time immemorial-until they had their eyes opened by the iniquities of the tariff. The letter goes on:
It contains 17 per cent to 19 per cent phosphorus and with 14 per cent guaranteed solu-able and available, and was to be delivered to us f.o.b. cars St. John, N.B., at $10 per ton. The Sydney slag advertised and sold throughout these two provinces only carries an analysis of 14 per cent to 16 per cent phosphorus with 12.05 per cent, guaranteed soluble and available to the farmer, or his crops. Just at this point this Nitrate Company informed of the impending duty, with the result that we deemed it prudent to reduce our order to 500 tons under such new conditions as we will have to pay the $5 extra in duty, in case they bring us Belgian slag, or a trifle less if British slag. Another addition to the hold-up in our efforts to increase the farm crops in this vicinity: Mr. Gutelius lately saw fit to give the Maritime farmers a further kick to the tune of 40 cents per ton additional cost in freight from either St. John or Halifax to Sackville. Some say this has again been slightly altered leaving the increase in freight over the Intercolonial at about thirty cents per ton.
Whilst Mr. Fawcett, a very intelligent man and an educated farmer, has his own views with respect to tariffs, and whilst he has been a Conservative, he is not in any sense a political partisan. He was in favour of reciprocity, believing in the interchange of natural products between this country and the people of tne United States. To the fact that the Conservatives in his community so believed, I owe my election in 1911 as a member of this House, because in that vicinity and in other sections of the country there were in 1911 at least fifty Conservative reciprocity men who voted not for me personally, but for the principle which I espoused, reciprocity. Mr. Fawcett took that view.
How did your majority compare with 1908? The hon. gentleman is making an assertion which the figures do not back up.

I have said that I owe my election to fifty reciprocity votes. Although I had a majority of 1,400 in 1908, I am free to say that had it not been for these votes I would not have been elected in 1911. I asked Mr. Fawcett if he had ever imported any of this slag in former years. He says:
Yes, in a small way we did last year, three carloads. It camel about as follows: The United Fruit Company of Annapolis valley quoted us Sydney slag at Halifax at $11.50 per ton, and added that they thought they could deliver it at Sackville at same figure, because freight rate, Sydney to Sackville, was the same as Sydney to Halifax. Later on they advised us they were unable to do so. Then we wrote directly to the Cross Fertilizer Company at Sydney asking them if they would deliver us three cars at Sackville at the $11.50. Mr. Walker, their manager, answered they could not deliver at less than the $11.50 Halifax price plus freight Halifax to Sackville, $1.20 per ton. Failing to see any justice or equity in thus being held up for two rates of freight Sydney to Sackville just because Sackville was unfortunate enough to be placed alongside of a railway instead of alongside St. John or Halifax or any other ocean port, we wired-
Hun. gentlemen can see the force of this statement. He has charged $11.50 a ton, the Halifax price, plus freight Halifax to Sackville but the Sydney concern made their price at Halifax to equal the price of the imported article, plus the duty at Halifax, plus the freight to Sackville.
-we wired Mr. Whlker again that we would take three cars of his slag delivered at Sackville at $11.50 per ton the same as he offered it to us at Halifax, same also as he offered it to us delivered at St. John even after he paid Intercolonial railway freight all the way from Sydney to St. John, otherwise if he refused us the slag at the competitive ocean port price

$11.50 we would give our little trade to the foreign slag which evidently was the only influence at keeping prices within the farmers reach.
Outside of this venture in slag we also imported about three other carloads of potash as it comes from Germany, nitrate as it comes from Chili and phosphate brought as it comes from the Southern States in proper proportions to mix in a complete fertilizer for potatoes and other crops of any analysis of 4 per cent nitrogen 2 per cent phosphorus and 10 per cent potash, After we got mixing these ingredients on our own barn floors we were visited by our New Brunswick Secretary of Agriculture (Mr. Daggett) with his expert chemist (Mr. Durst) who testified that our materials were so true to analysis that each ton was worth from $1 to $2 per ton more than any four by eight by ten mixture put up by any fertilizer manufacturer in the two provinces and sold to farmers at $40 to $42 per ton. We distributed our three cars among our neighbour farmers at $29 per ton which just paid labour and expenses of handling but no profit.
Now, there is the experiment of a practical farmer acting in co-operation with his neighbours, anxious to increase the production of their farm land, feeling the necessity of enriohing those lands with plant food, but not having available the natural manure on their farms for fertilizing purposes. They seek to get it at the cheapest possible price, at a price more in keeping with the value of the material, and co-operating, buy the ingredients which go to make up a commercial fertilizer, mix them on their barn floors and have a material that does not cost more than $29 a ton, a material that is, according to the testimony of the agricultural experts of the province of New Brunswick, better in fertilizing qualities than is the ordinary fertilizer purchased from the commercial fertilizer companies. It seems to me, without dwelling further upon the subject, that the action of the Government in attempting to extort secretly from the farmers this additional toll on their raw materials should be condemned. I have further said that the Customs Board were
9 p.m. not justified in passing that order, that it is illegal and improper and that it works very serious injustice to the farming community of the Maritime provinces particularly. I presume that wherever in Canada commercial fertilizers are in use there is a proportionate injustice and loss to the farming communities in those sections. I would therefore move, seconded by Mr. Hughes, of Kings, P.E.I.:
That under article 372 of the Customs tariff of Canada, 1907, blast furnace slag is on the free list, but that the Board of Customs, at a meeting held on the 9th day of September, A.D. 1913, improperly and illegally declared the same to be dutiable under tariff item 663

and in effect from the 9th of November, 1913, without such declaration being, as appears, approved by the Minister of Customs as required by statute and that the Department of Customs in now subjecting the same to duty is violating the statute to the great injustice and loss of the farming community.

Mr. Speaker, the situation appears to me to be something like this, that this Government, desiring to give the manufacturers of the country all the advantages that it is possible to give them, desiring to help them in every way even to the disadvantage of others, and not finding it expedient to raise the customs duties in the ordinary way, by increasing the tariff, have taken advantage of every possible excuse to do the same thing in another way, that is by rulings of the' Customs Board. This slag, as has been pointed out by the mover, is an ingredient in the compound of fertilizers and under the late Government it was admitted free of duty. By the tariff law of the country it was admitted free of duty. Some manufacturer in some part of Canada who treated this article in some way or other conceived the idea that it would be 'greatly to his advantage to have a duty put on it and apparently all he had to do was to see the Ministet of Customs, to see a member of this Government, and straightway a ruling of the Customs Board was obtained by which this article, which had hitherto been free, was subjected to a duty of 7 to 10 per cent.
That appears to be a peculiar way of helping the farmers, and this Government has often told us that its great desire is to help the farmers. It is something like the ruling of the Customs Board-putting a duty of $2 a thousand on lumber that had hitherto entered this country free. Rough lumber was admitted free, and under a ruling of the Customs Department of the late Government lumber planed on one side only was considered as rough lumber; but when this Government came into power, and when the present minister took charge of the Customs Department, he made a ruling subjecting that kind of lumber to a duty.
Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs). That is not right. I may say that rough lumber, or lumber planed on one side, comes in free, and has always been free.

It is free now, but it was
not free a year or two ago.

Yes, it was. It was only
dutiable when planed on both sides.

At all events, it is true that lumber that was admitted free by the late Government was, by a ruling of the Customs Board, made dutiable by this Government. Lumber is a necessity, almost a prime necessity, to the people living on the plains where lumber is very scarce. It is certainly raw material to the farmers, who have to build houses and barns for the protection of themselves and their stock, and the people who suffered loss by reason of that ruling brought their case to the Supreme Court of Canada, and as I understand it, the Supreme Court found that the ruling of the Customs Board was illegal, and ordered the removal of the duty which had been imposed by the present Minister of Customs. That is one of the things which show the insincerity of this Government when they state that they have the interests of the farmers at heart. They are willing to educate the farmer and do a great many things for him, providing he allows them to tax him all he can bear for the advantage of the manufacturers and the big interests. They are willing to pay professors, and the Lord knows how many men, to educate the farmer, and it is a peculiar education he gets, in some cases at all events. Some years ago a professor came down to my own province and told us that the very best thing the farmers could do was to establish cheese factories and manufacture cheese. He was a learned man and spoke well. The farmers thought he understood the business and took his advice. They established a great many cheece factories. But a few years after that another professor came along and said they had made a great mistake, that cheese farming was not the thing for them, and told them they should have gone in for making butter. He advised them to discard the machinery they already had in the cheese factories, and to install the very expensive machinery necessary for the making of butter. It has been well said that if you would get off the farmer's back, and allow him the freedom of working for himself, in nine cases out of ten he would be able to educate himself, and perhaps be able to give himself a better education than these high-salaried professors give him. If this Government were really sincere in its effort to help the farmer, it would at least give him his raw material free of duty, and lumber and fertilizer are raw material to the farmer, as has been pointed out. Why in the name of common sense, is an effort being made by the back door to tax this material that is so essential to
a farmer's existence? It seems to. me to be a very peculiar thing, but perhaps the minister may he able to explain it. It is just another indication that this Government wishes to put all the burdens it can upon the farming community for the benefit of the privileged classes, and for the benefit of the men whose orders they have to obey. It is well for the farmers to know the actual situation, and it is well that these things are occasionally exposed. This is an education that the farmers ought to get, and, so far as I am concerned, I will try to give it to them. If the minister has any explanation to make, I trust it will be a reasonable explanation; but there is one thing he cannot explain away, and it is this: that this article, which is of very great importance to the farmers of this country, came in free under the kat-e Government, and under this Government it is taxed to the disadvantage of the farmer and at the behest, I suppose, of somebody who thinks he can make a profit out of it.

I am very much surprised to see the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) pose as the farmer's champion. Last year when we had the Highways Bill before the House the hon. member did not pose as a champion of the farmer. This Government last year and the year before, put a large amount in the Estimates for the building of good roads for the farmers, and the hon. member for Westmorland was one of those who did what he could to prevent that money being expended.
Oh, no, you are wrong on that, as you are wrong on this.

The hon. mernoer's whole
argument was to show that fertilizers should be on the free list. In 1906, when the present tariff was being drawn up, the Hon. Mr. Fielding went into council, as every minister must do, and submitted that tariff for the approval of the Cabinet, and the hon. member for Westmorland sat at that council and approved of fertilizers being put on the dutiable list.
That was the tariff of 1907; I was not a member of the Government then.

November, 1906, was the time at which this tariff was passed, and the hon. member was a member of the Government and approved of a duty being placed on fertilizers, and placed, as he argues, to the disadvantage of the farmers of the country.
Now you have a chance to remedy it.
That may be, but the hon. member did not remedy it, and from 1906 until the present time he has never stood up in the House and advocated that fertilizers be put on the free list.
The farmers are asking for it, and you have the opportunity now; why do you not do it?

Now, this resolution states:
That under Article 372, of the Custom Tariff of Canada 1907, blast furnace slag is on the free list but that the Board of Customs, at a meeting held on the 9th day of September, A.D. 1913, improperly and illegally declared the same to be dutiable under Tariff Item 663.

Would the hon. member for Westmorland state that these blocks should be brought into this country and called blast furnace slag?
Why not?
It is changed into a manufactured article altogether.	.
No, it is only a new form in which it is brought in.

It becomes another article
altogether. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that corn is on the free list; if you simply ground the corn and brought the product in, would you still be allowed to bring it in as corn?
That is not a parallel case; you say that the slag is run into a mould.

with anything else when imported?

slag?

And mixing other ingredients with it.

My hon. friend may not know it, but this fertilizing company

has been in existence for a number of years, and this material has been imported free during that period.
They may have been doing that, and yet this concern would probably not find it out for some time.
They fix their price to suit the imported article.

As soon as they found that this was being imported, they notified the Commissioner of Customs. The matter was brought up before the Board of Customs, and they ruled that this was not blast furnace slag as intended by the item in the tariff, that it was being brought into this country as fertilizer, and that it should come under the item covering the article for which it was sold.
If those reasons made the Customs Board act, why does that not appear as a part of the record?

It is difficult for me to give an. answer to that, for the reason that the Customs Board has been in existence for years and years, the same men have composed that board, and they are the men who were there during the whole of the Liberal regime.
But they cannot be a law unto themselves.

It has been in existence all these years, l'ne power given to it by the Act has continued during the last fifteen or sixteen years. The carrying on of that Customs Board has not been changed in any way by this Government.
Not for twenty-five years, probably.

I do not know how long it is, but there have been no instructions given to them either by myself or this Government since we came into power. There has been no secrecy about these board meetings. There is a regular board meeting held once a month; others are called if necessary at any time. The hon. member asks why there were not some letters put in from some person showing that some charge was made that this article was being imported in this way. The answer is because the information was given verbally to the commissioner. Hardly- a week passes but some importer, or other person, comes to the customs and makes complaint that articles are either being charged too much duty or that parties are importing 41
goods at an under valuation, and so on. They made their complaint to the Commissioner of Customs, and he notified them on what day the board would meet. They appeared before the Board of Customs and stated their case, and the decision is recorded.	,
Is not a record kept?

Just as the hon. member
has a record of this.

There is no record
there.

We do not have a stenographer to take down the evidence of every little case. I believe the right hon.. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfried Laurier), the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and the hon. member for Ruesell (Mr. Murphy), will agree with me that the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) is wrong, because the Board of Customs have a precedent for this case. There was a case in -1909 almost similar to this where an appeal was made to the Board of Customs by a firm in Paris, Ontario. Here is the ruling of the Board of Customs:	.
The Board of Customs at its regular meeting on the 12th January, 1909, under the powers conferred by section 58 of the Customs Act, declared that broken gypsum rock not ground, per sample, such as would pass through a halfinch screen, is free of duty under item 292 of the Customs tariff of 1907.
This case was where a sample of crude gypsum had been submitted to the Board of Customs. It had not been ground fine like this slag, but it had been put through some machinery and broken up into smaller lumps so that it might be used, as I understand, in concrete work or work of that description. Here is the ruling of the Board of Customs:
It is admitted that the samples submitted have passed through a stonebreaker.
In this case, it has passed through a grinding mill and been made very fine.
Small samples were selected for decision, because if these were declared to be free of duty there would be no question as to duty on larger pieces of gypsum rock.
The Customs tariff, 1907, contains the following provisions as to gypsum rock and products thereof, viz.:
Item 292-Gypsum, crude, sulphate of lime, free in all the tariffs.
Item 294-Plaster of Paris or gypsum, ground not calcined-Preferential tariff, 10 per cent: intermediate tariff, 125 per cent; general tariff, 15 per cent.
Item 293-Plaster of Paris or gypsum, cal-



cined, and prepared wall plaster, the weight of the package to be included in the weight for duty, per 100 pounds-Preferential tariff, 8 cents; intermediate tariff, 11 cents; general tariff, 121 cents.
The board held that the meaning of 'crude' in item 292 was ' raw,' not ground, refined or calcined. If the breaking of gypsum rock into small pieces is held to be a manufacture, the broken gypsum rock would fall under item 208 at 30 per cent general tariff, as manufactures of stone, n.o.p., while the ground gypsum, a more advanced article of commerce, is only 15 per cent under the general tariff.
' Crude ' is a term usually applied to articles in a rough state-not finished or refined.
Raw materials in earth, clay, sand, rock, etc., are as a general rule free of duty in the tariff of 1907, vide following items free in all tariffs,
' Item 296-Refuse stone, not sawn, hammered or cfiiselled, nor fit for flag stone, building stone or paving.
Item 295-Clays, including China clay, fire clay and pipe clay not further manufactured than ground:	ganister and sand; gravels;
earths, crude only.
Item 296-Flint, ground flint stones; felspar, flourspar, magnesite; soap stone, cliff, chalk, China, or Cornwall stone, ground or unground.
Item 297-Silex or crystallized quartz, ground or unground.
The Alabastine Company, jnmited, cite a decision by the United States appraisers rating crushed gypsum as ' An article manufactured in whole or in part, n.o.p,,' under section 6, United States tariff, 1897.
There is no similar provision as to duty in the Canadian Customs tariff of 1907.
Crude gypsum is on the free list in Canada but not on the United States free list.
Was there an appeal?

Yes, here is the decision of council:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council was pleased to hear an appeal front the Alabastine Company, Limited, of Paris, Ontario, against a decision of the Board of Customs on ' the 12th of January, 1909, declaring broken gypsum rock not ground, per sample, such as would pass through a half-inch screen, to be free of duty under item 292 of the customs tai'iff as gypsum ' crude.'
His Excellency in Council, having heard arguments in favour of and against the said appeal, was pleased to over-rule the said decision of the Board of Customs, and to order and declare, under sections 62 and 63 of the Customs Act, that the duty on gypsum, as above set forth, is payable under item 294 of the customs tariff as gypsum, ground, not calcined.
(Sgd.) P. R. Bennetts, Assistant Clerk of the Privy Council.
That is an appeal from the Board of Customs to the Governor in Council, and there were present at that council meeting Sir Richard Cartwright; Mr. Fielding, the framer of the tariff; Mr. Paterson, the Minister of Customs; Mr. Templeman, Mr. Brodeur, Mr. Oliver, from the West, who is

also looking after the interest of the farmers; Mr. Lemieux, Mr. Pugsley, Mr. Graham and Mr. Murphy. If that decision was right, then surely the blast furnace slag that is taken rough from the mills, taken to another concern altogether, then ground and made into an entirely different article of commerce, would come under item 294, that is, would be dutiable. If it was allowed to come in free, it came in without the knowledge of the Customs Department. So far as the Government were concerned, we knew nothing about it. It came up in the usual way before the Board of Customs. After they had given a ruling on it, the matter was submitted to me with all the explanations. I certainly approved of the ruling.
If an article is not specified in the tariff, the Board of Customs has been appointed and has always been in existence to interpret under what item that particular article of which the complaint has been made should be placed. There is no such item in the tariff as basic ground slag. For that reason it should come under the item under which it is sold. So far as I am informed by the Assistant Commissioner of Customs, all this fertilizer is imported from England or Belgium, and the rate of duty is simply five per cent.
Were any representations made by the Cross Fertilizer Company of Sydney as to the comparative prices of their product and the product that came over from England?

As I understand it, the Cross Fertilizer Company stated to the commissioner that the price that they were charging before the decision of the board has not since been changed. There has been no advance in price.
How is it that the man who imported the article has to pay the duty on it now ?

There is a ruling of the Board of Customs. At all events, having the duty added to the price, as stated by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), at 5 per cent would be but 50 cents a ton. This is all that could possibly be added even if the manufacturer at Sydney took advantage of the price. But he has not taken advantage of it; the price has not been raised since the interpretation by the Board of Customs ?
It is 10 per cent from Belgium, not 5 per cent.

The preferential rate is 5 per cent. The commissioner told me today that the importation has been from England, and 5 per cent is the rate which applies. The hon. member for Westmorland has been making a mountain out of a molehill. He has gone into several other matters-the high cost of living, the freight rates on the Intercolonial railway, and so on. I will not attempt to answer him on these subjects to-night. I think the explanation given should be satisfactory to the hon. member. In future, if he is to bring forward a case for the farmers, I hope he will have a better one than this which he has brought before us this evening.
Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N.B.) * After the very elaborate explanation given by the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid), I suppose he thinks that the last word has been said, and therefore that it is presumptuous on my part to attempt to discuss this matter. Nevertheless, so long as I am here, I shall have to take the opportunity to say a few kind words, especially when a matter affecting the administration of my hon. friend the Minister of Customs comes up. We appreciate the position in which the minister finds himself to-night, and I am not surprised that he speaks of this matter as he does-a mere 50 cents a ton to be paid by the farmer on fertilizer. Of course, the minister thinks that not worth talking about. But I may tell the minister if he were a farmer in New Brunswick and probably handling from twenty-five to forty tons of this material, he would find this duty quite a little item. And the duty does not mean merely an increase of 50 cents a ton, but by the time you add two or three profits it amounts to $1 a ton. Of course, the hon. minister thinks in millions now, and he does not care about what the farmer has to pay for fertilizer. He has talked about pretty nearly everything except the subject under discussion. He started talking about my hon. friend from Westmorland preventing the spending of money on the roads. That is outside the question, of course, but to put the minister right, let me quote from the record of my hon. friend from Westmorland, and also from the record of the Minister of Customs, on this question of the roads. Last session the Government, in the goodness of their hearts, saw fit to' make a proposition to give $1,500,000 to the country under certain conditions for the benefit of the highways, and provided 411
that it should be expended under the Canada Highways Act. On the 4th of June, I think it was-possibly on the 3rd of June-the Senate of Canada made an amendment to the Highways Bill which this House would not adopt, as was stated in this House by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways. This was on the 4th of June. On the 5th of June-	,
